newsitem.title: USA: Alternate juror dismissed at Simpson civil trial.
newsitem.headline: Alternate juror dismissed at Simpson civil trial.

text.p: An alternate juror who apparently wrote in a Christmas card to a friend that he was on the O.J. Simpson civil trial was dismissed from the case on Tuesday.
Earlier a forensic expert backed down on his testimony in the civil trial that two assailants may have murdered Simpson's ex-wife and her friend, conceding that the facts pointed to only one killer.
When the 12-person jury and alternate jurors returned after the lunch break, one of the five remaining alternates -- a Hispanic man in his 40s -- was missing.

Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki, who has banned TV cameras in a bid to avoid the kind of circus atmosphere that surrounded Simpson's criminal trial, did not refer to the dismissed alternate juror specifically.
But he told the remaining jurors: "You'll note one of your number is no longer with you. You are not to speculate as to the reason."

After reminding the jury they could not discuss the case among themselves or with anyone else, he hinted at why the alternate was booted. "People may know you are on this case, but your duty is not to initiate any conversations," the judge sternly admonished them.

A source close to the case told Reuters the alternate juror had written in a Christmas card to a friend that he was on the celebrity case. The friend, who is a deputy sheriff, notified court officials and the man was dismissed.
The dismissal leaves just four of the original eight alternates in addition to the regular jury.

Simpson was acquitted in October 1995 of criminal charges in the murders of his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman. He is fighting a wrongful death lawsuit by the victims families, who are seek monetary damages.

Before the alternate juror was dismissed, Michael Baden, a New York State Police forensics expert, gave testimony for a second day. Baden had testified on Monday he reached the conclusion that more than one assailant was involved because "it would have been very difficult for a single perpetrator to control multiple victims in a public place."
But asked on Tuesday by plaintiffs' lawyer Edward Medvene, "Would it be fair to say that based on the facts you know of, that the facts are consistent with only one assailant?"
Baden replied, "It would be consistent with one person."
Medvene then asked, "It would be your testimony that all of the knife wounds are consistent with being delivered by one knife?"
Besides backing down on the two killer scenario, he also said under cross-examination that the fatal wounds suffered by Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman were consistent with one knife.

Baden, who was called by Simpson's defence in the civil case and who also testified on the ex-football star's behalf in his criminal trial, backed down on his previous insistence that Goldman struggled with his killer for five to 10 minutes before finally succumbing to his wounds.
He said Goldman may have stayed alive for only "two to three minutes" after receiving his fatal neck wound.
The length of the struggle is important because lawyers for the plaintiffs contend the murders were committed outside Nicole Simpson's condominium at about 10:35 to 10:40 p.m. on June 12, 1994.
O.J. Simpson was spotted in his driveway by a limousine driver at about 10:55 p.m. The less time it took to commit the murders, the more time he had to get back to his mansion two miles away.
